facts.one_liner: Wildlife, wild coast and the Remarkable Rocks.
facts.why_go: Kangaroo Island is Australia’s third-largest island and a wildlife haven. Australian sea lions rest on the beach at Seal Bay, and kangaroos, wallabies, koalas and echidnas are common. In Flinders Chase National Park, the Remarkable Rocks are wind-sculpted granite boulders on a dome above the sea.
facts.how_to_get_there: Ferries from Cape Jervis; flights from Adelaide.

facts.one_liner: Volcanic peaks, black-sand beaches and Papeete’s market.
facts.why_go: Tahiti is the largest island of French Polynesia, a volcanic island of rainforest-covered peaks and black-sand beaches. Papeete’s market sells pearls, tiare flowers and local food. Teahupo’o is one of the world’s most famous surf waves and hosted the surfing at the 2024 Olympics.
facts.good_to_know: Tahiti is the gateway to Moorea and Bora Bora.

facts.one_liner: A Swahili town of dhows and donkeys.
facts.why_go: Lamu Old Town is the oldest and best-preserved Swahili settlement in East Africa and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. There are no cars on the island, so donkeys and dhows remain part of daily life, and narrow lanes lead past carved wooden doors.
facts.how_to_get_there: Flights to Manda Island, then a boat.

facts.one_liner: Jagged peaks rising from Arctic fjords.
facts.why_go: Senja, Norway’s second-largest island, is known for its jagged peaks rising straight from the sea. The hike up Segla gives one of the most famous views in Arctic Norway, and the National Tourist Route along the outer coast passes fishing villages and fjords.

facts.one_liner: Arctic glaciers, polar bears and the world’s northernmost town.
facts.why_go: Spitsbergen is the largest island of the Svalbard archipelago, high in the Arctic between mainland Norway and the North Pole. Longyearbyen is one of the world’s northernmost towns, with the midnight sun in summer and polar night in winter. Glaciers, walruses, reindeer and polar bears can be seen on guided tours.
facts.best_time: March–May; June–August for the midnight sun.

facts.one_liner: Vineyards and beaches a ferry ride from Auckland.
facts.why_go: Waiheke Island, in Auckland’s Hauraki Gulf, is known for its vineyards, olive groves and beaches like Oneroa and Onetangi. Wineries serve long lunches, and coastal walks and art galleries make it an easy day trip.
facts.how_to_get_there: Ferries from Auckland take about 40 minutes.

facts.one_liner: Sea stacks, medieval churches and Visby’s walls.
facts.why_go: Gotland is Sweden’s largest island. Its capital, Visby, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site encircled by medieval walls. On Fårö, limestone sea stacks called raukar stand on the shore, and film director Ingmar Bergman lived and worked there.

facts.one_liner: Neoclassical houses climbing from a colourful harbour.
facts.why_go: Symi is a small Dodecanese island whose harbour, Gialos, is lined with colourful neoclassical mansions climbing the hillside. The Monastery of Panormitis is an important pilgrimage site, and quiet coves can be reached by water taxi.

facts.one_liner: A car-free island of sand streets and whale sharks.
facts.why_go: Holbox is a car-free island off the north coast of the Yucatán Peninsula with sandy streets, colourful murals and shallow turquoise water. From June to September, whale sharks gather offshore to feed, and flamingos are seen in the lagoon.
facts.best_time: June–September for whale sharks; November–April for dry weather.

facts.one_liner: Croatia’s most remote inhabited island: fishing villages, wine and sea caves.
facts.why_go: Vis lies farther out in the Adriatic than any other inhabited Croatian island and was a Yugoslav military base closed to foreign visitors until 1989, which kept it unspoiled. Its two towns, Vis and the fishing village of Komiža, sit on deep bays backed by vineyards. Boat trips run to the Blue Cave on the nearby islet of Biševo, and the island’s rugged coast hides coves such as Stiniva.
facts.best_time: June and September for warm seas and fewer boats; July–August is lively.
facts.how_to_get_there: Car ferries and catamarans from Split take roughly 1.5–2.5 hours.
facts.good_to_know: Rent a scooter or car to explore—buses are infrequent. Visit the Blue Cave in late morning for the best light.
